title: Update: I ran the full 245-day backtest. My strategy lost 99.54% — and trading costs weren't the only problem.
author: BlackGreep
selftext:
A while ago, I shared a 7-day backtest of a crypto trend-pullback strategy.

The result was +$506 gross, but −$1,183 after modeled trading costs. Several people correctly pointed out that 31 trades weren't enough to establish an edge.

So I kept the strategy unchanged and ran a much longer Discovery test.

\*\*Setup:\*\*
- BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT, SOLUSDT
- Bybit linear perpetuals, 1-minute data
- May–December 2025 (245 days)
- $10,000 starting equity
- 0.055% taker fee per side + 0.02% modeled slippage per side

\*\*Results:\*\*
- 979 closed trades
- Gross P&L: −$176.58
- Fees: −$7,169.78
- Modeled slippage: −$2,607.19
- Net P&L: −$9,953.55 (−99.54%)
- Final equity: $46.45
- Profit factor: 0.15

Every month and every instrument was negative after costs. Even more interestingly, 102 of the 341 take-profit exits ended up losing money after fees and slippage.

We independently reconciled all 979 trades and over 2.1 million accounting points. The financial arithmetic checked out.

\*\*The main finding:\*\* the strategy wasn't just too expensive to execute. Its aggregate gross P&L was negative even before trading costs.

This is still a provisional historical simulation: funding is unverified, historical venue specifications aren't fully validated, and liquidation isn't modeled. OOS and Holdout have not been tested.

I'm building BlackGreep around reproducible strategy validation, and this is exactly the kind of failure I want the system to catch before anyone risks real money.

For those working on systematic trading: what would you examine next in a failure this severe — trade economics, risk behavior, or the underlying signal hypothesis?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Posting a result like this is rare, and the clean split between gross and net is helpful. Since gross was negative too, I'd look at the signal first. Compare its entries with random entries that use the same exits and holding time, to see if the signal adds anything. If it doesn't, tuning exits or costs won't rescue it. After that I'd check which hours and market states did worst, and whether fewer trades aiming at bigger moves would pay for the fees. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is built for similar checks, with a fee setting and a held out stretch of data.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Thanks — I agree that signal quality should be investigated first.

A random-entry baseline with comparable exposure and causal exit rules sounds like a useful next diagnostic. I'd be careful not to reuse future exit information when constructing that comparison.

We also want to examine performance by hour and market regime using the Discovery data, without tuning the original strategy.

OOS and Holdout remain untouched. Appreciate the suggestion!

comments.author: QATSAlgo
comments.body: The reconciliation is a useful step forward. I would separate signal quality from sizing next: rerun the unchanged entries and exits with fixed notional, then compare gross return per unit of turnover across months. Near-total loss can combine a weak signal with sizing that keeps consuming the remaining equity. Also show gross target distance versus the 0.15% modeled round-trip cost; those 102 net-negative TP exits deserve their own row. Keep OOS untouched until that diagnosis is complete. QATS team here; commenting on validation.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Good point about separating signal quality from position sizing.

The 245-day Discovery ended with $46.45 remaining from $10,000. Gross P&L was −$176.58, while modeled trading costs totaled about $9,777. And 102 of 341 TP exits were still net-negative.

Looking at gross performance per unit of turnover across months and running a fixed-notional diagnostic should help us understand the interaction between weak signals, shrinking equity, and sizing.

We'll clearly distinguish that diagnostic from a full replay, since changing notional also affects margin and admission constraints.

OOS is still untouched. Thanks for the methodological feedback!
